choice: JSONL for services, basicConfig for single-file tools

Measured: hand-rolled JsonlFormatter + configureLogging is 21 lines per file, byte-identical across all four programs, 84 lines total and 8% of the arm - so a one-shot CLI emits machine-parseable stderr no machine reads. The stdlib has no JSONL formatter, so every self-contained program re-pastes it. Decide by who reads the logs: a service, or anything whose logs are collected, imports JSONL from a shared module and never re-pastes it; a single-file tool run by hand uses logging.basicConfig. The event-name and extra={} discipline is unchanged in both cases; only the formatter goes.

choice: repeated calls to one callee are one block
note: DERIVED from a false positive found in the length experiment. NAR008 split two adjacent parser.add_argument(...) calls purely because the first wrapped past three lines - breaking exactly the grouping the rule exists to protect. It was a syntactic proxy (statement span) for a semantic property (logical self-containment). Fixed: consecutive expression-statements calling the SAME callee are treated as one block. Verified no change to any existing file's count.

options: contract complexity: raises, >3 params, or over 20 lines
choice: contract complexity
note: A pure line threshold is gameable in the wrong direction - splitting a 21-line function into two 12-line ones deletes the obligation, so the rule rewards fragmentation. Contract complexity does not shrink when a function is split: the pieces still raise and still take their parameters. Measured impact of the change across 13 written files: 0-4 new findings each, 24 total, and every one inspected was legitimate - e.g. transitionTo raises IllegalTransitionError with nothing telling a caller so. It also caught Finding in checks.py, a pure data holder with a hand-written 4-parameter __init__ that the style says should be a frozen dataclass; converted.

choice: only positional parameters count
note: Clarification of R2b-B1 and the original doc rule: the >3 threshold applies to args, not kwargs - a function can have lots of kwargs. NAR003 now counts posonlyargs + args and ignores kwonlyargs. This also supplies the escape hatch the rule previously lacked at exactly four parameters, which was the standing critique: put `*` before the optional ones and they stop counting, which documents them as optional anyway. NAR004 deliberately still counts EVERY parameter, keyword-only included, because each is part of the contract even when the caller may omit it.

choice: report unreadable files as NAR000
note: DERIVED from a crash during verification. checks.py tracebacked with FileNotFoundError on a missing path, and again in the summary line which re-read every file to compute a rate. A linter invoked over a directory must not stop at the first bad path - that is the degrade-and-report rule (Q24) applied to the tool itself. Both fixed: unreadable and non-UTF-8 files now report as NAR000 findings and the summary skips them.

choice: measured
note: DERIVED measurement, answering what NAR009 and the contract-complexity NAR004 cost. Retrofitting ten files added 402 lines, of which 117 fell in the four length-experiment programs. The code count over that experiment stayed at exactly 572 before and after, which proves the additions were pure documentation and independently corroborates the reported 402 insertions with zero deletions. Against unguided Claude the style now measures 27% more total lines and 6.5% less logic. On task t3 the Narrative version is shorter in total than the unguided one.

options: basicConfig with a standard format string
choice: a 7-line field-rendering formatter
note: DERIVED from a cold-start agent that followed the rules and shipped worse logs than an f-string would have given. R5-03 scoped JSONL to services and told a single-file tool to use logging.basicConfig(format=...). That contradicts Q08: the standard formatter discards everything in extra={}, so LOG.warning('merge.rejected', extra={'rejected': 4812, 'total': 10000}) prints only `WARNING merge.rejected`. The R4-02 tally rule exists so an operator can act on '4,812 of 10,000 rejected', and the prescribed formatter destroyed exactly that number. Verified both the failure and the fix. A 7-line FieldFormatter renders the fields, against 21 lines for the JSONL formatter that R5-03 rejected as too costly.

options: counts plus the failing tool's output
choice: counts plus the failing tool's output
note: DERIVED from a cold-start test. verify.py printed `1 findings` with no file, line or rule id, while SKILL.md and README both said 'do not call the tools by hand'. Acting on a failure therefore required disobeying the instruction, and the tester did so on the first round. A gate that forbids the only route to detail will be ignored. verify.py now prints each failing tool's own output under a header.

choice: --violations is required, not optional
note: DERIVED while testing R5-10. verify.py omitted --violations, which the README documents. Without it vermin fails any file it cannot date: a file using no version-specific syntax reports `~2, ~3` with 'Not enough evidence' and vermin treats that as target-not-met, exit 1. Verified all three cases after the fix - evidence-free file passes, conformant file passes, and datetime.UTC is still caught as 3.11. This was a false-failure generator in the shipped harness.

options: check the config carries the Narrative sections
choice: check the config carries the Narrative sections
note: DERIVED from an adversarial review, and the third instance of one bug class. verify.py checked only that pyproject.toml existed. Every real project already has one, so present-but-wrong is the DEFAULT state rather than an edge case: a file containing only [project] gave `ruff check clean` on a module with snake_case functions and double quotes. verify.py now parses the config and requires [tool.ruff] line-length, [tool.ruff.lint] select, [tool.pylint.basic] function-naming-style and [tool.mypy] strict, naming what is absent. It also passes --config through to ruff and --config-file to mypy, which it previously gave only to pylint, so the flag did nothing for two of the four tools.

choice: # noqa: NARxxx
condition: the comment goes on the line the finding reports, which for a function-level rule is the def line
note: DERIVED. checks.py had no suppression of any kind, so a false positive was unfixable and verify.py would exit 1 forever. Worse, NAR001 fired on LOG_PATH.write_text(...) because 'write' was a mutating prefix, and the only way to clear it was a `global LOG_PATH` that lied about a side effect - destroying the exact signal the marker carries. Two fixes: 'write' and 'load' dropped from MUTATING_PREFIXES because a Path is a value and writing a file mutates no module state, and a noqa mechanism added because every check here is a heuristic over syntax and each one can be wrong.

choice: state the caveats with the number
note: DERIVED from an adversarial review that called the headline an aggregation artefact. Correct. Per task the code delta is t1 +6, t2 +6, t3 -37, t4 -15, so Narrative wrote MORE logic on half the tasks and the 6.5% aggregate rests entirely on t3 and t4. The sample is four with one run per cell and no variance measured. The Narrative arm was also edited after the run, because the module-docstring rule landed later and its retrofit added 117 lines, so the 1144 total is a post-hoc artefact rather than a one-pass result. The code count did not move across that retrofit, which is why it is the figure to trust. The README now carries all three caveats.

choice: snake_case
note: Module filenames are snake_case, unlike functions and methods which stay mixedCase. The shipped pylint config set seven naming styles and omitted module-naming-style, so pylint silently applied its snake_case default and rejected a mixedCase module. SKILL.md's own docstring example used loadCsv.py and therefore failed the gate it documents. Config now sets module-naming-style explicitly and the example reads load_csv.py.

options: one pipeline covering code and prose
choice: one pipeline covering code and prose
note: Cited the Zen of Python: there should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do it. An agent must not reason about workflow at run time. verify.py now takes any path, sorts .py from .md, runs the six code checks on the first and the STE linter on the second, and reports one line per check. Prose over 2.5 violations per 100 words fails. The STE skill is a soft dependency, so its absence reports as skipped rather than as a failure.

options: ban every ORM that validates at runtime
choice: ban every ORM that validates at runtime
note: Stated rationale: validation is supposed to be solved before user data enters the database, not after. The config previously banned only pydantic and sqlalchemy.orm, so peewee, tortoise, sqlmodel, pony and django.db.models all passed - verified. Added sqlmodel, peewee, tortoise, pony, ormar, piccolo, sqlobject and django.db.models, each with the reason in its message.

choice: pin exact versions
condition: pin whatever can be replicated; agent judgement calls cannot be
note: Stated reason: exact replication of results. The install command previously installed the newest version of each tool while the README table claimed four specific versions, and resolveToolchain accepted any binary on PATH. Ruff moved [tool.ruff.lint] in 0.2, so an unpinned install changes what the config means. requirements-lock.txt now pins ruff 0.16.3, pylint 4.0.7, mypy 2.3.1 and vermin 1.8.0, and both the README and verify.py's error message point at it.

choice: document what each family demands
note: DERIVED from an adversarial review. The config enabled UP, SIM, RET, PTH, LOG and G on one uncommented line, and no document said what they require. PTH123 bans open(), PTH118 bans os.path.join, and RET504 forbids a named value before return - so conformant-looking code fails on rules nobody stated. Each family now carries a comment naming its sharpest rule.

choice: disable RET504
note: RET504 forbids a named value before `return` and demands `return handle.read()` over `text = handle.read(); return text`. A named intermediate often tells the reader what is being returned, so the rule works against the reader-effort principle the style is built on. Third entry in the ignore list justified on the demand being wrong rather than the autofix being dangerous, after SIM114 and SIM103.

options: ban ORMs on the hot path only
choice: ban ORMs on the hot path only
condition: lifted under maintenance/, scripts/ and migrations/
note: Refines R6-03, which banned every runtime-validating ORM outright. Stated position: an ORM is an excellent tool for database healing scripts, and should not be on the hot loop such as a webapp endpoint returning database values. The objection is per-request cost, not the tool. Implemented with ruff per-file-ignores rather than prose, so the boundary is enforced rather than advised. Verified: peewee is banned under src/ and clean under maintenance/.

choice: walk ast.List so callables are measured
note: DERIVED and verified. annotationDepth recursed only through ast.Subscript, and a callable's parameter list is an ast.List, so the SAME type was flagged as a plain parameter and invisible inside Callable[[...], None]. The rule therefore depended on where a type appeared rather than on how deep it was. Fixed by walking ast.List without charging a level. Verified: Callable[[dict[str, list[tuple[float, float]]]], None] now reports depth 4, and the conformant corpus stays at zero findings.

choice: comprehension and shared vocabulary
condition: data gets a dataclass; a callable gets a Protocol
note: Settles what NAR005 is for, after measurement showed its stated remedy catches no bug. Stated test is conversational: could you refer to this type in a normal discussion with another programmer? `park(car: Car)` reads and discusses, `park(car: dict[str, list[tuple[float, float]]])` does neither. A deep Callable is the same smell with a different fix - Callable[[dict[str, list[tuple[float, float]]], Mapping[str, Sequence[frozenset[Path]]]], None] should be a Protocol. Verified that neither tuple[float, float] nor a Point dataclass makes mypy --strict catch swapped coordinates, and only NewType does, so the rule must not be sold as type safety. checks.py now names the remedy by kind.

choice: keep NAR008 as written
note: The dict-literal case needs no rule change. Two reasons given. First, the blank line is correct: defining a record and serialising it are logically distinct operations. Second, the real fault is upstream - a large dict should not be passed around, so it should be a frozen dataclass and then the exploded literal never appears. Supporting evidence from the comparison: the reference implementations already hit this shape 11 times and paid the blank line each time without complaint, and the # fmt: off fence sanctioned by R2b-B2 already dissolves the case where the literal must stay packed.

options: depth and width, with the remedy chosen by type
choice: depth and width, with the remedy chosen by type
note: Corrects R6-09, which read the Protocol remedy as depth-driven. Depth is one threshold for deciding something should be spun out, not the only one: tuple[a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j] resolves to depth 1 and still wants a dataclass because of the number of depth-1 arguments. NAR005 now fires on depth over 2 OR width over 3 at any single level, and the TYPE then chooses the fix - a Callable becomes a Protocol, anything else (any kind of iterable) becomes a dataclass. Verified zero regressions across the conformant corpus, and the width trigger caught a genuine case in the unguided control arm: Sequence[tuple[str, str, Any, Any]].

choice: TODO defers, FIXME blocks unless the code is orphaned
note: Sharpens the original doc, which said only that FIXME marks a failure to meet standards and TODO marks non-urgent debt. TODO is deferred work and never blocks a merge. FIXME means one of two things: a merge blocker when it sits in code that runs, or a danger sign when it sits in code nothing calls - a known correctness problem parked in an orphaned section, for whoever next thinks about adding it to the hot loop. Only the first is a defect, and reachability separates them, so this is checkable. NAR010 walks the call graph from main and from module level and flags a FIXME inside a reachable function. It over-approximates reachability deliberately, preferring to call an orphan live over letting a running FIXME through. Verified: a FIXME in a called helper fires, the same comment in an uncalled function does not, and TODO never fires.

options: gather the model (one file per hardware model)
gather the flow (one file holds the whole journey)
depends on the ratio of the two events
choice: neither -- a change lands at exactly one abstraction level
note: Rejected the axis. Both options counted files touched, from opposite ends, and neither is the measure. The stated design was readers/common/poller.py for the general probing method (exponential dropoff or direct waits), readers/acme/vendor.py for the vendor byte format, readers/acme/x200.py for device-specific unpacking importing from vendor.py, and the same shape under readers/tesla/. Stated benefit, verbatim: 'the abstraction levels are clear, and errors / changes are localized to their abstraction level (oh, the vendor releases a new format? ok, I fix at vendor.py)'. So the measure is not how many files a change touches, it is whether the KIND of the change identifies the one place it lands. A vendor format change, a device quirk and a probing-policy change are three kinds and each has exactly one home. This supersedes both offered metrics and is the scoring rule the rest of round 7 inherits. Note the device imports the vendor, never the reverse, which is also a dependency-direction datum for block A.

choice: the split follows how much work the level does, not a fixed line count
condition: stated as assumptions behind R7-M01, not measured against code
note: SUPERSEDED by R7-B01-B03-criterion: a coherent concern earns a module and line count is not the criterion. The numbers below describe how big a concern usually is in that domain, not a test. Original record follows. Three thresholds named while answering R7-M01. First: the per-device file is justified when it produces a full parsed dataclass, which was estimated at hundreds of lines. Second: if the device work is trivial, around 10 lines because the program only passes buffers through as a library, then several vendor devices in one file is acceptable. Third: past roughly 800 lines for a single device, refactor again, into an x200/ directory with an __init__.py that hides the complexity from the consumer. Recorded as weak and derived because the numbers were estimates offered in passing rather than read off real programs, and because the repository standard is that NAR003's 3 and NAR004's 20 both came from measured code. Block B must ask these against real files before any of them ships as a rule.

options: one more parameter threaded through three functions
choice: dearest is the threaded parameter, then the file, cheapest is the named type
note: Verbatim: 'C >> A >> B'. A named type is not a cost at all here: observed_at is a property of the reading, so it does not make sense to put it anywhere other than with the thing it is associated with. The one stated escape hatch is an insane performance benefit from an external scheduler, given as 10x or 100x on the most expensive part of the hot loop. A threaded parameter is the dearest of the three because feeding in variables that are not used costs mental RAM for the human developer that does not pay off, and two of the three functions in the example never used the clock. Consequence for the rest of the round: a design that adds a named type to remove a threaded parameter is strictly better, and a design that adds a file to remove a threaded parameter is also better. NAR005's remedy of naming an inner type is therefore cheap by this measure, and R2b-E3's rule that 5+ parameters means a missing state dataclass is reinforced from a second direction.

options: store imports config and looks the device up
the caller passes the looked-up device down
choice: depends
condition: A when the device the reading was taken on is a property of the reading; B when it is not
note: SUPERSEDED by R7-A01-revised, which replaces the vague "property of" condition with a stated test. Original record follows. Verbatim: 'A is preferred here, solely based on the assumption that the Device the Reading is taken on is a property of the Reading. If the Device is not a property of the reading, then B is preferred.' So the arrow between two modules is decided by whether the callee already owns the thing it would look up, not by a fixed layer order. Unasked third option worth noting: if the device genuinely is a property of the reading, the sharper answer is that Reading carries the DeviceEntry and neither module looks anything up. Neither offered option contains that, so the question under-covered its own axis.

options: dissolve the shared type into primitives
choice: a shared vocabulary module
note: Provocation landed. Verbatim: 'it is better to have a common types file instead of do circular import handling. Circular import handing is bad because it spends a bunch of unnecessary mental RAM.' Ranked B > A > C. C rejected on responsibility grounds rather than on type loss: 'the choice of which values get pulled out is recordOutcome's responsibility, not finishOne's.' That is a general principle and is the more portable half of the answer -- a callee that takes primitives has pushed its own destructuring decision onto every caller. The TYPE_CHECKING fix is cheap because the future import is mandatory, and cheapness is exactly why it gets reached for; the cost it hides is the reader's, not the interpreter's.

options: the workflow function opens the database
the entry point opens it and passes it down
choice: the entry point opens it and passes it down
note: Verbatim: 'the most natural entry point for a DB open is at the very start of the relevant code flow, which means it should always be at runService rather than pollForever (because the lifetime scope is the service, not the polling)'. Stated goal: avoid accidentally opening a lot of database connections. The rule generalises past the database -- a resource is opened at the scope whose lifetime it matches, and the reader finds the open at the top of that scope. Separately raised and NOT settled here: whether a connection held open across idle periods is itself wrong when writes arrive every five minutes rather than continuously. Called a feeling about unnecessary resource utilisation and explicitly left open for a harder question.

options: one errors.py holding the whole tree
a shared base, each leaf in the module that raises it
choice: a shared base, each leaf in the module that raises it
note: SUPERSEDED by R7-A04-revised. The answer REVERSED from B to A once the crossing case was made concrete. Original record follows. Verbatim: 'B is preferred for locality / abstraction reasons. With A the human is context switching a lot while reading it, with B the human is not.' Direct application of R7-M01: the kind of change names the level, and a new refusal mode in the parser is a parser change. Read with R7-A02, which put a SHARED type in a common module: the two are consistent, not contradictory, and the reconciliation is recorded as R7-A02-A04-ownership.

choice: a type lives with its owner; it moves to a shared module only when more than one module owns it
note: SUPERSEDED by R7-A04-revised. The owner-count reconciliation below is wrong: errors go central preemptively, not on owner count. Original record follows. Reconciles R7-A02 and R7-A04, which chose opposite homes for a type in the same block. PollOutcome went to a shared vocabulary module because store and poller both handle it. CorruptFrameError stayed in the parser because only the parser raises it. The distinguishing fact is the number of owners, not the fact of being a type. A type read by many but owned by one stays with its owner. This is the module-scale form of R3a-12's constant-placement test and it inherits that test's honesty problem: ownership is a judgement, and a checker counting importers will flag the shared vocabulary module the style prescribes.

options: a copy on each side with a comment
the writer imports from the reader
choice: a third module both import
note: Verbatim: B is 'horrible, this is a complete violation of DRY and a great source of future bugs'. C rejected on the same ground as the circular import: 'the responsibility logic should flow down a hierarchical tree ... Reader and writer are at the same logical level, so having one import from another feels wrong.' The shared node is a new sibling beside them, not a move into the parent: 'The file protocol is part of the IO system, so it is the logical place to put it.' Two participants that must agree on a byte layout are the clearest case, because a drift between the copies is a bug no type checker and no linter reports.

choice: judgement, not lintable
note: Probed with three edge cases after the answerer asked to be pushed. Case 1 settles it: io/reader.py importing io/checksum.py in the same directory is FINE, because checksum is below reader whatever the directory says. Directory depth is therefore not the level, and the sibling rule is not a rule about directories. A declared layer table was offered and rejected too. Case 2: the frame format stays in io.protocol and a consumer elsewhere imports it, because the format is part of the IO system and does not stop being so when something else wants it -- but the specific example was itself judged a design defect, because a renderer has no business reading raw bytes. Consequence for the checker: no NAR1xx rule can enforce this. It is a review rule and must be written with the admission SKILL.md:167 already uses. The answerer stated flatly that this reasoning is not yet specified enough to ship to SKILL.md, so it is recorded as evidence and must not become a rule without further probing.

choice: one common.py per system first, split into common/ when it grows, types before implementation
condition: scoped to one system's directory, never a project-wide utils.py; thresholds unmeasured
note: Answer to the proliferation case, where following the sibling rule literally turns three modules into six. Verbatim: 'The problem with huge amounts of files is it becomes difficult to reason about for the human. In general I would start with a common.py file, and if it gets too long, then I would worry about splitting it into a common/ folder with multiple files. The first logical split would be types/definitions vs. implementation, then after that, multiple implementation files. In general DRY must be preserved, and if reader/writer are doing the same retry, that violates DRY.' Note what this does NOT license: this common.py is scoped to one system's directory, so io/common.py holds what io shares. It is not the project-wide utils.py that R7-B04 asks about, and the two must not be conflated. Recorded weak because 'too long' has no number and because it partially contaminates R7-B04 and R7-B07, both of which are now non-blind.

options: each module registers itself at import
one module names every model in an exhaustive match
choice: one module names every model in an exhaustive match
note: Provocation refuted, as R4-03 predicted. Verbatim: 'B reads as much cleaner and more easy to work with mentally.' The registry inverts the import arrows and buys extensibility with a mutable module-level dict that nothing type-checks; the match arm fails the type check when a member is added. Worth recording that the answer came on readability, not on the type-safety argument, so it is independent evidence for the same conclusion rather than a restatement of R4-03.

options: leaf modules import the constants they need
one module-level CONFIG rebound at startup
choice: leaf modules import the constants they need
condition: A when the constants are known at import; B when the config is resolved at runtime, as when a machine config is executed, dumped to .env and read back
note: C excluded strongly and separately, on the ground that a high-level config file for global program functioning and tuning is the right shape, which a rebound module global is not. Between A and B the preference is A, on explicitness: 'a file that relies on DATABASE_PATH and RETENTION_DAYS is obvious from the import list, but in B it is not obvious.' The caveat is real and self-reported: with seven machine configs tracked in git, loaded by executing a python config, dumping to .env and reading it back with decouple, the values are not known at import and A may be impossible. Recorded weak for that reason. Consistent with R7-M02, which prices a threaded parameter as the dearest of the three costs, and B threads one.

options: poller collects per-device failures, service logs the aggregate
poller lets it propagate, service catches and exits
choice: poller collects per-device failures, service logs the aggregate
note: CONTROL, and it passed only on the second asking. The first answer was B, given as 'high level interfaces should be simple, powerful, and concise' -- a judgement on option B's one-line comprehension, not on its failure behaviour. The question was defective: the round's preamble promises every pair is behaviourally identical and this pair was not, because B exits the daemon when one of forty instruments is unreachable. Re-asked with that consequence stated and the answer moved to A. Q24 therefore survives the move from a batch CLI to a long-running service unchanged. Two lessons for the rest of round 7: an option whose behaviour differs must say so in the question, and a control that fails must be re-asked before its block is voided, which is what key.md pre-registered for this one.

options: store imports config and looks the device up
the caller passes the looked-up device down
choice: store imports config and looks the device up
condition: whenever the callee can derive the extra input from what it already receives
note: Replaces the 'is it a property of the reading' condition, which was not a test. The stated rule is about caller burden, verbatim: 'I do not like requiring the callers to send duplicate information when it could already be inferred from the existing inputs. That leads to complicated interfaces and complicated usages. In this case, reading contains the device pointer, which allows looking up device info. This is busy work that insertReading should handle, not the recordOne caller.' On the offered test: site_code is a property of DeviceEntry, not of Reading, so denormalising it onto the reading is rejected and a device_id -> DeviceEntry lookup is correct. Two consequences. First, this agrees with R7-M02, which prices a threaded parameter as the dearest of the three costs; passing a DeviceEntry the callee could look up is exactly that parameter. Second, it OUTRANKS the dependency-direction instinct: store.py importing config.py is accepted, so 'do not make the caller do work the callee can do' wins over 'keep the arrow out of the lower module'. Record that ordering, because the two rules collide often.

options: one errors.py holding the whole tree
a shared base, each leaf in the module that raises it
choice: one errors.py holding the whole tree
note: REVERSAL. R7-A04 first chose B on locality grounds. Asking the follow-on -- what does service.py catch when protocol.py raises -- reversed it. Verbatim: 'Sorry, I take it back. A is preferred for R7-A04, because errors are part of the vocabulary of the entire program. Something else might catch said error and so the types need to be in a higher up location to avoid circular imports.' Two things this settles. First, an exception type is not owned by the module that raises it, because a handler can be anywhere, so an error is shared by construction and the owner-count test does not apply to it. Second, the reason is circular-import avoidance, which is the same cost R7-A02 already refused to pay -- so this is that decision applied a second time rather than a new one. Instrument lesson, and the more important half: a question about where a type LIVES gives the wrong answer if it does not also show the type CROSSING. Placement looks like a locality problem until you watch a handler two modules up try to name the type. Every remaining placement question in round 7 must show the crossing.

options: hold it open for the service lifetime
depends on what is behind the handle
choice: depends on what is behind the handle
condition: hold a local file handle open; do not hold a handle that costs something on the other side
note: Follow-on to R7-A03, asked because the answerer flagged an unresolved feeling about resource utilisation and invited a harder question. The resolution is that idle TIME is not the variable. A sqlite3 connection is a local file and a buffer, so holding it costs nothing and closing it would move the open away from the top of its scope, which R7-A03 settled against. A network database, a device socket or a licensed vendor SDK handle is different in kind: it has a server-side timeout, a connection limit or a seat, so an idle hold can fail silently somewhere the program cannot see. The rule is what the handle costs on the far side, not how long it sits unused.

choice: a fact lives in the module that is about the thing the fact is a property of
note: The rule that replaces the level question, arrived at from code in benchmark/round7/programs/level_test/. Verbatim, on why a per-vendor retry cap must not sit in a generic backoff module: 'The timeout setting is a property of the manufacturer's networking stack, not a property of the backoff program.' The word 'leak', which the interviewer had been using, was rejected as not carrying an intuition. Ownership does. It subsumes three earlier round-7 answers that looked unrelated: R7-A01-revised put a site_code lookup with DeviceEntry because site_code is a property of DeviceEntry; R7-A04-revised put exception types in the shared vocabulary because an exception is a property of the whole program, any module being able to catch it; and the log-field finding put the field set with whatever emits the record. The reuse test and the domain-change test both turn out to be indirect ways of asking the ownership question, which is why they agree exactly when the fact is already in the right place. Measured: adding a third vendor touched 3 files with the cap misplaced and 2 with it owned, and the misplaced version forced an edit to the module a reader would call generic infrastructure.

choice: measure what the edit must know, not how many files it touches
note: Independent code support for R7-M01, which rejected both file-count metrics when they were offered in the abstract. Two of the three variants touch the same number of files to add a vendor, and they are not the same design. The fixed/ edit writes the wire format, the magic bytes, the reading and the device id into main.py; the owned/ edit writes the word bosch twice. A reviewer of the owned/ diff does not need to know what a Bosch is. A reviewer of the fixed/ diff must check that '<4sf' and b'BSCH' are right and has nothing in main.py to check them against. File count scored these equal and is therefore the wrong instrument. This also sets the scoring rule for the remaining stage-2 clusters: report what each variant's diff has to know, not only how many files it spans.

choice: the entry point knows which modules exist and nothing about any of them
note: Verbatim: 'I do not really like that main.py has device info to begin with - it should be in the acme/tesla/bosch files. Main should not need to know details of the devices, only collect their interfaces.' This rejected the interviewer's own fixed/ variant and produced the owned/ variant, in which each vendor module publishes one VendorReader carrying its devices, its reader and its recovery time, and main.py holds only VENDORS = (acme.VENDOR, tesla.VENDOR). The Protocol used to type the reader is earned rather than speculative: two real implementations exist, which is R2-01's stated test, and no test double is involved. Note the floor: something must still name the new module, so two files is the minimum for a new vendor and one is not reachable without an import-time registry, which R7-A06 already rejected.

choice: order module-level constants by who changes the value, tunable first, developer-only bindings last
note: Raised against owned/acme.py in benchmark/round7/programs/level_test/, where DEVICES sat below the function definitions next to VENDOR. Verbatim: 'in acme/tesla, DEVICES are user input constants, which means it needs to go at the top of the file with other constants. VENDOR is a code interface thing and would only normally be changed by the developer, so it going at the bottom of the file is fine.' This sharpens two rules the style already has. R3a-12 asks whether someone could change a value knowing only what the program DOES, and uses that to decide module level against function local; the same question also decides ORDER within the module-level block. SKILL.md already separates tunable constants from design-baked globals with a blank line, and the real criterion behind that separation is who does the changing, not global against constant. Note the collision and its resolution: DEVICES is the most operator-facing constant in the file, so it wants to be first, but its value references ACME_FORMAT and RETRY_CAP_S, so module execution order forces it last inside the block. It joins the constant block rather than leading it. That is R4-03's precedent exactly -- ordering is forced by execution and you do not contort around it. Three-part shape for a library module that follows: tunable constants, then the functions, then the interface binding that names them.

options: two files, split only where a second program needs the code
choice: six modules of 40 to 90 lines
note: Provocation 'never split' REFUTED. Verbatim: 'B is easier to reason with lower RAM than A. It gives you mental buckets you can slot groups of functions into.' A 340-line service becomes six modules, so the single-file affordance that SKILL.md is built around -- main() first, workflow in call order, vocabulary last -- does not extend past one file's worth of program. C, the split-only-on-a-second-consumer position, was recognised and rejected as triage: 'this is a fairly common way I might do it in practice, but this is only because I am doing triage where the tech debt hurts the most. I do not think it is what I would pick given infinite time.' That is the round's own framing applied by the answerer unprompted and it is evidence the instrument is measuring what it claims to.

choice: by technical layer
condition: for this program; the general rule is to cut on whichever axis the expected changes land in more cleanly
note: Verbatim: 'A (sort by conceptually related functionality) makes the most sense. The problem with B is that it is elegant once, but will be very messy if you decide to refactor program flow. A handles this gracefully with minimal LOC changes.' Asked again against level_test/owned/, which cuts by SUBJECT (acme.py, tesla.py) and was approved, the answer was that there is no structural rule: choose whichever axis a change lands in more cleanly. So R7-B02 records a result for one program rather than a general axis, and the general rule is R7-M01 applied directly. Recorded weak for that reason. The apparent conflict with owned/ is not one -- that program has three subjects and this one has a single wire format and a single database, so it has no second subject to separate.

options: the same four names live in store.py
choice: a 28-line retention.py exists
note: Verbatim: 'A is an elegant cut point and great for keeping logically related functionality together.' Twenty-eight lines earns its own module when it is one coherent concern. Read with R7-B01, which split 340 lines six ways, the two are consistent and both point away from size as the criterion. See R7-B01-B03-criterion.

choice: a coherent concern earns a module; line count is not the criterion
note: Reconciles R7-B01 and R7-B03, which sit at opposite ends of the size axis and agreed. Twenty-eight lines earns a file when it is one concern; three hundred and forty lines is six files because it is six concerns. Neither answer referred to a number. This SUPERSEDES the size thresholds recorded weak as R7-M01-sizes, which were estimates offered in passing: around ten lines per device, a full parsed dataclass, around eight hundred lines before a directory. Those numbers describe how big a coherent concern usually is in that particular domain; they are not the test. The test is whether the block of code is about one thing that can be named without saying misc.

options: each helper in its only caller
a named module for the shared one, the other two stay local
choice: naming a concept and crossing a boundary are the same test
note: First pass was unresolved and said so: 'I like A, putting truly common / implementation agnostic functionality into utils is a good sign of a competent developer (anticipating future shared functionality). But it does reduce the ability to put related functionality into mental buckets (reducing developer RAM), which C is best at. Maybe some combination of A and C? I think it needs more judgement calls before this is specific enough to be workable.' The follow-on offered two candidate tests -- does the helper name a concept, and does anything outside the package use it -- and the answer was that they are one test. A helper that crosses a boundary must be findable by someone who did not write it, which forces it to name a concept; one that never leaves does not. So crc32Of earns checksum.py and humanBytes and chunked can share a common module inside the package. NOTE THE UNTESTED PREDICTION: the two tests are claimed identical and no case where they disagree has been built. Build one before this ships as a rule.

options: facade plus a shared constant and a shared logger
choice: re-export facade with __all__
note: Provocation 'empty __init__.py' refuted. Verbatim: '__all__ is good practice for libraries, but I am not familiar enough with its usage to recommend between B and C. If I understand it is for public interfaces, and FRAME_BYTES and LOG are not public interfaces of scanlib.' The stated understanding is correct -- __all__ declares the export surface, controls star imports, and is what type checkers and documentation tools read -- so C falls on the answerer's own reasoning rather than on an outside argument. Recorded WEAK because the answerer flagged unfamiliarity, not because the reasoning was thin. Consistent with the R7-M01 remark that an 800-line device becomes a directory with a friendly __init__.py that hides complexity, which was the first sign this would not come back empty.

options: from collector import store, then store.insertReading
choice: from collector import store, then store.insertReading
note: Verbatim: 'B increases clarity and is regularly used such as import numpy as np and import matplotlib.pyplot as plt.' This extends R3a-08 from third-party to first-party modules: import the class, keep the verb qualified. store.insertReading keeps the module where it carries meaning, exactly as struct.unpack and json.loads do. One thing the cited analogy carries that the answer did not: numpy and pyplot are imported UNDER AN ALIAS, and the style has no rule about aliasing a first-party module. The chosen form has no alias. Whether `from collector import store as store_module` or `import collector.store as store` is ever wanted is unasked.

options: the package glossary holds every type, crossing or not
the glossary holds what crosses, a single-module type stays home
choice: the package glossary holds every type, crossing or not
note: Reframed before asking, because R7-A02 and R7-A04-revised had already settled the crossing case. What was left was whether a type used by exactly ONE module also goes central, which is where R7-A04-revised and R7-A05-property genuinely disagree. R7-A04-revised wins. Verbatim: 'it could be reasonably expected that other future scripts will want to look at the FrameHeader output, so putting it in vocabulary makes sense. If it is likely to be read by other scripts, moving it pre-emptively to common is a good idea.' The criterion is a forecast, not a count of current importers, so R7-A02-A04-ownership's owner-count reading is dead for types. See R7-B07-preemption.

choice: a type may be centralised before it is shared; behaviour may not be generalised before it is needed
note: Unifies two round-7 answers that pull in opposite directions on speculation, and the split between them is the finding. Types are centralised PRE-EMPTIVELY: exception types went to the shared module because anything might catch them (R7-A04-revised), and FrameHeader went there because a future script might read it (R7-B07). Behaviour is NOT generalised pre-emptively: the registering decorator that would accept any future model was refused in favour of an exhaustive match naming the two that exist (R7-A06). The asymmetry is defensible on cost. Moving a type later changes every import of it and is a mechanical, reviewable edit that a type checker verifies; a wrongly-general dispatch mechanism is load-bearing and its removal is not mechanical. This is a departure from the round's grug calibration and should be written as such rather than smoothed over.

options: __all__ declares the surface, every name spelled the same
choice: leading underscore on internals
note: Verbatim: 'If functions are meant to be internal, they should follow A notation.' The style had NO privacy convention before this; the corpus contains no leading underscore and no __all__. Read with R7-B05, which put __all__ in a package __init__.py, the two are not alternatives: __all__ declares a package's export surface and the underscore marks a module's internals. A checker can enforce the pair exactly -- a cross-module import of an underscore-prefixed name is a mechanical finding with no judgement in it -- which makes this one of the few architecture answers in round 7 that is lintable.

options: service.py holds main and __main__.py re-exports it
choice: __main__.py holds main
condition: until main grows long, at which point the workflow splits out and __main__.py keeps the entry
note: First answer was A with an objection to the filename: 'It should not be called __main__.py, I generally think of dunder methods as internal machinery, not something user facing.' The objection rests on a factual gap, corrected in the follow-up: __main__.py is the exact filename Python executes for `python3 -m collector`, so it is not a naming choice. Response: 'oh interesting, I was not familiar with this module entry method. I assumed you always had do something like python3 -m collector.main. Ok, I like __main__.py. Generally it should hold the primary entrypoint for the module, but if it gets too long it can be split out to another file.' The dunder never reaches a user, who types the package name. Original reasoning stands: 'The point of the main entrypoint is to define the logic, I do not see much point in splitting it into a service unless main gets really really long.' A console-script entry point was offered and not chosen.

options: exempt until the second public function
choice: exempt until the second public function
note: CONTROL FAILED, and unlike R7-A08 the re-ask CONFIRMED the departure rather than returning to the doc. First pass chose B, but the question was defective in the same way A08 was: option A carried both the module docstring and the little-endian detail, option B carried neither, so the answer was about where the DETAIL goes. Verbatim first pass: 'the fact that the function parses a little-endian header should be part of the function description always. If the file has only a single function, the file-wide docstring can be skipped.' Re-asked with the detail held in the function docstring in both options, the answer was the exemption with a stated trigger: no module docstring while there is exactly one public function, mandatory the moment a second appears. This is a CHANGE REQUEST AGAINST NAR009, which today fires on any module with no docstring. Scope to settle before it is implemented: the exemption is for the docstring clause only, and a runnable module must still carry its usage example, so the exemption presumably applies to non-runnable modules. The trigger is mechanically checkable -- count public defs -- which is why it was preferred over the unbounded version. No checker change is made in this round; the acceptance gate requires a cost measurement first.

options: one public function, underscore names do not count
one public function and also short
choice: one function of any kind
note: Scope for the NAR009 exemption R7-B10 requested. A module containing exactly one def is exempt from the module-docstring requirement, whether that def is public or underscore-prefixed. The second def, of any kind, makes the docstring mandatory. Reasoning implicit in the choice over the narrower option: two functions is where a module starts being ABOUT something rather than DOING one thing, and that is the moment it owes a sentence. The line-count variant was rejected, consistent with R7-B01-B03-criterion having just removed size as a criterion. Checkable exactly by counting FunctionDef and AsyncFunctionDef at module level. Still unsettled and NOT decided here: whether a runnable module is exempt, since NAR009's other clause demands a usage example from anything with a __main__ block. Settle that before checks.py changes.

choice: any module-level name
note: Scope for the underscore convention chosen in R7-B08. It marks any module-level name -- functions, constants, classes, type aliases -- so _FRAME_FORMAT and _FrameHeader are as legitimate as _unpackFields. A module FILENAME does not take the underscore; the third option offering _helpers.py was not chosen. The churn objection was put and rejected on its own terms, verbatim: 'I reject the framing of costs churn: a name that becomes public later gets renamed at every call site. If it is getting called in a bunch of places, it is public, not private.' That reply is the more portable finding. The underscore is a statement of present fact, not a forecast, so a name whose fact changes SHOULD be renamed and the rename is the correct signal rather than a cost. Contrast R7-B07-preemption, where a TYPE may be centralised on a forecast -- the asymmetry is that centralising a type is reversible mechanically and a privacy claim is not a claim about the future at all.

choice: __main__.py holds it and __init__.py stays empty
note: Answers what replaces the single-file reading order once R7-B01 splits a program into six modules. The thesis stays with main(): __main__.py opens with a docstring naming what the program is for and listing the modules in reading order, and every other module keeps its own one-line docstring. The stated model, verbatim: 'My understanding is __init__ is for startup stuff that needs to run as a consequence of module import. __main__.py is new to me, I hadn't heard about it, but it more or less seems to replace what I previously had as main.py.' Known and accepted cost: a reader arriving at store.py from a stack trace or a grep sees one line about that file and nothing telling them five siblings exist or where to start. Most readers do not arrive at the entry point. The alternative of a back-pointer per module was offered and not chosen. See R7-B01-init for the checker consequence.

choice: an empty __init__.py needs no docstring; NAR009 needs a second exemption
note: Found by building rather than by asking, which is the GAPS.md method. benchmark/round7/programs/six_modules/ is the first program in this repository with an __init__.py, and checks.py immediately reported collector/__init__.py:1: NAR009 module has no docstring. The repository contains no other __init__.py anywhere, so NAR009 had never met one. An empty __init__.py is the ordinary correct thing for an application package once R7-B01-map puts the reading order in __main__.py. Note this is NOT covered by the exemption in R7-B10-scope, which is worded as exactly one def; an empty __init__.py has none. So NAR009 now carries two pending change requests: exempt a module with exactly one def, and exempt an __init__.py. Neither is implemented in this round -- the acceptance gate requires a cost measurement first. Contrast R7-B05, where a LIBRARY package's __init__.py is a re-export facade and does carry a docstring; the two are not in conflict, because that one has content.

options: it must appear in a signature first
name it but leave it local
choice: it must appear in a signature first
note: Bounds R7-B07, which said types centralise pre-emptively and which taken literally would send every shape in a program to the glossary. It does not reach the three values struct.unpack produces inside parseFrame. Verbatim: 'The struct is never observed anywhere else, only inside parseFrame. As long as the output has guarantees on typing, it is kosher.' So the test is mechanical and checkable: a shape that appears in a parameter or return annotation is a type the program has and centralises; a shape built and consumed inside one function is a step, not a type. This keeps the glossary an inventory of what modules pass between them rather than of every intermediate value, and it reconciles R7-B07 with R7-A05-property -- a purely internal shape is a property of the function that builds it.

options: ruff format's form: 4-space continuation, closing paren at column 0
hanging double indent: 8-space continuation, closing paren at 4
choice: hanging double indent
condition: BLOCKED -- unimplementable with the pinned toolchain, so the shipped style remains ruff format's form
note: Stated unprompted while reading benchmark/round7/programs/six_modules/collector/poller.py: the preference is 8-space continuation for parameters with the closing paren and return arrow indented 4. PEP 8 explicitly blesses this form, to distinguish arguments from the body, and the reason is real -- under ruff's form a parameter line and the first body line sit at the same indent, which is the confusion the extra indent exists to prevent. VERIFIED BLOCKED. ruff format rewrites the preferred form to its own and exposes no setting for it, being Black-compatible and Black having deliberately no continuation-indent knob. Three ways out, all costly. Switch formatters, which breaks tooling.md's ownership split and R6-02's single-pipeline decision, and changes behaviour everywhere else too. Fence every multi-argument signature with # fmt: off, which R2b-B2 licensed for a rare packed literal and which would here be pervasive. Or accept ruff's form. Recorded as a genuine preference that the toolchain overrules, because a preference silently dropped is how a style doc starts lying. NAR003 is unaffected: it requires one positional argument per line above three and says nothing about the indent.

options: fence every signature with # fmt: off
choice: accept ruff format's form
note: Resolution of R7-indent. Verbatim: 'I will just accept ruff format's form I guess. It's fine.' The preference for a hanging double indent stands on the record and is not withdrawn; what is settled is that it does not justify switching formatters or fencing every multi-argument signature. Recorded separately from R7-indent so a future reader does not re-open the formatter question: it was asked, the cost was priced, and the constraint was accepted. tooling.md's ownership split and R6-02's single pipeline survive unchanged.

options: no Protocol, name the concrete class
choice: no Protocol, name the concrete class
note: CONTROL PASSED, first time, no re-ask. Reproduces R2-01 across a module boundary. Verbatim: 'If there is no anticipated future usage of ReadingStore, it is pointless to create a Protocol for it beforehand. It just reads as duplicated code, which is a DRY violation.' The DRY framing is an argument R2-01 does not carry -- a Protocol over the only implementation restates every method signature, so it is a cost paid now rather than a benefit merely deferred. Offered as an addition to the rule and REJECTED as a restatement: 'The Protocol fails in this case because it is only consumed by one thing. Adding another statement saying it violates DRY would be strictly true, but also be a unnecessary duplication of the same problem description.' That refusal is itself the style's one-word-for-one-thing principle applied to its own rule text, and it is why R7-C01-C02 states one test rather than two.

options: the store is an object built at startup and passed down
the store is a module of functions taking the connection
choice: the store is an object built at startup and passed down
note: Provocation REFUTED. The proposition was that if one implementation does not earn a Protocol it may not earn an object either. It does. Verbatim: 'A is preferred because a database bring up and bring down has an associated lifetime and entry/exit method, so scoping it inside a class makes sense.' The class is justified by lifetime ownership, not by polymorphism, which is why it survives alongside R7-C01 refusing the Protocol. Consistent with R7-A03: the entry point still opens the resource and passes the object down.

choice: a class is earned by owning a lifetime; a Protocol is earned by a second real implementation
note: SUPERSEDED by R7-C01-C02-revised. The lifetime-ownership criterion below was REJECTED: 'I do not think R7-C01's conclusion of objects can only exist if they own a lifetime is right.' The half about Protocols stands. Original record follows. Reconciles R7-C01, R7-C02 and R7-C08, which chose no-Protocol, yes-object and real-dependencies in the same block. Two separate tests that look similar and are not. A class exists because something has a bring-up and a bring-down, or state that must stay consistent, and something must own that. A Protocol exists only when a second real implementation exists, and a test double is not one (R2-02). So the single-implementer check proposed for arch_checks.py would be the RIGHT check for Protocols and the WRONG one for classes, and any such rule must say which it counts. The alternative reading, that the object is justified by cohesion rather than lifetime, was offered and not chosen.

options: each stage decides and calls the next
one coordinator calls each stage and holds the intermediates
choice: one coordinator calls each stage and holds the intermediates
note: Verbatim: 'verifyAndStore and storeAndReport are not going to be reused anywhere else, so splitting it like this adds a bunch of argument passing and function signature for no reason.' Direct application of R2-09 (extract on foreseen reuse, not on nameability) and of R7-M02 (a threaded parameter is the dearest cost). CONFOUND, self-reported and real: 'verifyAndStore and storeAndReport are not great function names or logical cut points, which is biasing me against A.' Both are and-names, which signal a function doing two things, so option A was weaker than the dimension it was meant to test. The stated exception survives the confound and is the portable half: 'I can see splitting a clearly logically disconnected complicated piece in a function to keep an implementation clear.' So chained delegation is refused for a pipeline whose stages are arbitrary cuts, not for a genuinely separable piece.

options: the flag stops at the level that can act on it
choice: the flag stops at the level that can act on it
note: Verbatim: 'Sending arguments to functions that do not use them is generally a waste of mental RAM (unless they are wrapped in a larger config).' Restates R7-M02 from a third direction and confirms it at module scale. Note the parenthetical, which is the seed of the R7-C05 question: bundling several such values into one named config is an accepted escape from the cost, and it is what makes a context object defensible where a loose parameter is not.

options: a pure decision, then one executor
choice: a pure decision, then one executor
note: Provocation LANDED, reversing the round-3 P1 result at a size where the plan record pays. Four routing rules and three effects. Verbatim: 'I like B a lot more, it separates out the logically coherent pieces.' Round 3 ranked the pure-core variant THIRD, and the recorded reason there was about global state rather than about purity, so this is the first clean test of the axis. Read with R7-C07, which refuses the same split at a smaller size: the pair yields a threshold rather than a flat rule, which was the stated aim of asking twice.

options: build the line where it is emitted
choice: build the line where it is emitted
condition: extract once the formatting carries logic rather than one f-string
note: The small end of the axis R7-C06 tests at the large end, and the answers SPLIT, which was the desired result. Verbatim: 'At this size, B is fine, but if renderRound were doing a bunch of unwieldy logic rather than a simple f-string, it may make sense to do A.' So the pure-core split is not a flat rule: it is earned by the amount of decision-making in the pure part. One f-string is not a core. Four routing rules is. R2-09's one-line-helper-called-once-is-residue is the same judgement at function scale, and this extends it to the pure-core pattern.

choice: a real temporary database
note: CONTROL PASSED, first time, no re-ask. Reproduces R2-02 in a question that also changes the production signature from a connection to a store object. Verbatim: 'A is preferred as it exercises real functionality. A test can drift from the underlying implementation, you never want to be testing your test harness rather than the real code functionality.' Note the answer went to A while R7-C02 chose the store OBJECT, so the vote is against the double specifically and not against the seam -- the two are consistent, and the reconciliation is R7-C01-C02.

choice: if a general name for the group is hard to pick, it is not a real grouping
note: R7-C05 as asked was rejected as an instrument: 'I do not really understand how Collection is a clear descriptor of something that holds both a SQL connection, a device mapping, and a path. Since this dataclass sucks, I am biased towards A, but I think that just indicates that this test is a poor discriminator.' Correct, and the failure is the finding. Verbatim on the reframe: 'if picking a general name is really hard, it probably isn't a proper grouping.' This is the guard rail R2b-E3 lacks. That rule says 5+ parameters means a missing state dataclass; it does not say what to do when the five do not name anything, which is the common case. Whether the remedy is then a better-named bundle or a missing OWNER is unsettled -- see the open note on R7-C05.

options: not where the name only echoes
choice: only the last return
condition: the size at which it starts to matter is unmeasured; the reasoning was given for a 50-line function
note: Raised unprompted while reading benchmark/round7/programs/six_modules/. The preference is `plan = RecordPlan(...)` then `return plan` over returning the constructor call. RET504 forbids exactly this and is ALREADY DISABLED (R6-06), on reasoning the answerer re-derived independently -- a named intermediate tells the reader what is being returned. So unlike R7-indent this preference is implementable; the config permitted it and no rule stated it. Asked as always / only-where-informative / only-the-last-return, and measured first against the running program: 13 of 14 returns would gain a line under always, including three near-identical `outcome = ...` / `return outcome` pairs inside one function, which manufactures the rote diffing R2b-P0 exists to prevent, and `read = sum(...)` inside a property already named read. The answer narrows to the FINAL return only, and the stated reason is orientation rather than naming: 'if a function is 50 lines long, figuring out what the return type should be requires scrolling all the way back up to the function signature. If there is simply a descriptive name at the end then it is clear what it is supposed to be returning.' Early returns and guard exits are therefore exempt, which removes the three-identical-pairs cost entirely. Mechanically checkable -- a checker can tell the final statement of a body from an early exit. OPEN: the reasoning is about a long function and no threshold was set, so whether a three-line function's final return needs a name is unsettled. NAR004 has the precedent, requiring a docstring once a body runs past 20 lines.

options: values that could differ between instances
the group has a domain noun
choice: values that could differ between instances
note: Replaces the lifetime-ownership criterion of R7-C01-C02, which was rejected, and the shared-state criterion offered next, which was rejected as too loose: 'I like shared state several operations need but I do not think it is anywhere near specific enough. Every file would be a class under this rule.' Correct -- almost every module has functions sharing a topic and some values. The criterion that survives: a CLASS when the values come from outside and the program could hold two of them at once, a MODULE when the values are constants of the program. ReadingStore qualifies, because two connections can coexist. RetentionPolicy qualifies, because per-site policies can coexist. protocol.py does not, because FRAME_FORMAT and MAGIC are the same everywhere. checksum.py does not. The Protocol half of R7-C01-C02 is untouched and still stands: a Protocol is earned by a second real implementation and a test double is not one (R2-02). Note this also DISSOLVES an apparent conflict. The class for retention was first justified by flexibility to future retention work, which would have contradicted R7-B07-preemption -- behaviour may not be generalised before it is needed, which is what killed the registering decorator in R7-A06. Instance multiplicity is a fact about the program now, not a forecast, so no exception to B07-preemption is required.

options: every bundle is a missing class
choice: find the owner; the owner is a class when its values could differ between instances
note: The forced choice as put was malformed and was called out: 'C and B here are not mutually exclusive options since they do not work on the same code.' Correct -- the two rewrites applied to two different signatures, so they could never compete. The synthesis, once the class criterion of R7-C01-C02-revised is in hand: a long parameter list is a missing OWNER, not a missing record. Find what owns the values. That owner is a class when the program could hold two of it, and a module otherwise. pollOne(connection, devices, status_path, device) becomes pollOne(store, device) because a store owns all three and two stores can coexist. pruneOldReadings(connection, retention_days, prune_batch, now) becomes a method on RetentionPolicy for the same reason. This rewrites R2b-E3, which says 5+ parameters means a missing state dataclass: it usually means a missing owner, and the dataclass is only the answer when nothing has behaviour over the values. The naming guard rail from R7-C05-naming still applies -- if a general name for the group is hard to pick, it is not a real grouping.

options: the module qualifier counts toward the name
the name is wrong, not the scope
choice: name what the function produces, not what it takes
note: Raised unprompted: 'cutoffFor is not clear enough to make it obvious what it is doing if you saw it without context in another part of the codebase ... I prefer verbose function names generally speaking.' Offered as a scope question -- does retention.cutoffFor count as the name, given R7-B06 makes every call module-qualified -- and the answer rejected the framing. The defect is not that the name is short or unqualified. cutoffFor says what the function takes; it should say what it returns, which is the instant before which readings are deleted, so deleteBefore or oldestReadingToKeep. Verbosity was the symptom the answerer reported and naming the RESULT is the cure, so lengthening a label is the wrong fix. This is new. choice: a blank line separates logical steps, at any nesting depth; length is not the trigger

choice: paste a real sample of the output and delete the prose
condition: costs lines in four cases of five; the sample goes stale and no tool catches it, which is accepted on the same terms as the __main__.py map
note: Raised by the author reading the V4 full arm, AFTER round 9's first pass had already cut style-guide justification from docstrings. The remaining defect is milder and separate: the docstring explains where it could show. Verbatim complaint: 'Often times, the actual thing explains much more than restating what it does in natural language.' MEASURED across both V4 guided arms: every module that READS a format pastes a sample of that format, and every module that PRODUCES text describes it in prose instead -- summary_table.py, overages.py, logs.py and byte_size.py all carry a prose description of their own output and no sample of it. The cause is R3a-11's condition, which scopes the show-an-example rule to 'file moves, copies, path manipulation', so both arms read it as covering input formats only. Resolution generalises it: where a module reads or writes concrete text, paste a real sample and DELETE the prose the sample replaces. Two further cuts were taken from the same complaint. First, the summary line names what the module produces by its real name -- 'construct a QuotaPolicy' beats 'answer what it states about a team and about a path', which paraphrases a type that already has a name. Second, stop at the fact: 'The first malformed field stops the read.' is the rule, and the sentence explaining why stopping is right is not functionality. That second cut extends R9-02, which banned style-guide justification; this bans justifying the design at all inside a docstring, and sends a surviving reason to a # comment at the line that needs it. Worked example in SKILL.md is the author's own rewrite of full/quotas.py, which took a 12-line docstring to 8. MEASURED AFTER WRITING THE RULE, and it refuted the reason first given for it: pasting the sample took five module docstrings of the V4 full arm from 5, 5, 6, 8 and 13 lines to 19, 9, 8, 9 and 10. Only quotas.py got shorter, and only because it was the one carrying paraphrase and justification. The sample buys exactness and not brevity, so the rule states that cost rather than claiming a saving it does not deliver. TIGHTENED after the author reviewed five worked before/after pairs. THREE amendments. (1) NEVER INVENT A SAMPLE. Verbatim: 'Never ever invent data or formatting from thin air under any circumstances - this is untruthful. Showing records / repr is fine.' Found by the author in this repository's own demonstration: overages.py computes records and renders nothing, and the first rewrite gave it a compact table that appears nowhere in the program -- a format invented to satisfy the rule, which is the failure R9-01 names one level out. A module that computes rather than renders pastes the repr of what it returns. (2) SHOW ONE LINE OF EACH SHAPE, not the whole output: one team row, one over-quota line, one file outcome, no repeats. (3) STALENESS IS ACCEPTED AND STATED: a pasted sample drifts and no tool catches it, which is the cost R9-02 already accepts for the __main__.py module map, so the rule says to keep the sample small and re-paste it when the output changes rather than pretending the cost is absent.

options: write for a professional developer, and drop STE
choice: write for a professional developer, and drop STE
note: SUPERSEDES R6-02's one-pipeline-for-code-and-prose and R8-D34's loud-skip behaviour. It AMENDS rather than supersedes R5-02: that decision chose 'full program docstring in STE with usage examples', and only the STE clause dies. The requirement for a full program docstring with an example invocation per mode stays in force and NAR009 still enforces it. Raised by the author rejecting 'A program that does not run the command-line tool calls reconcileDirectory' in favour of 'Provides reconcileDirectory API', with the reason: 'It is perfectly fine to use programmer jargon, professional developers will be working on this codebase.' A FIRST ANALYSIS CLAIMED STE'S CONTROLLED VOCABULARY BANNED THAT JARGON. THAT WAS WRONG AND IS RETRACTED. Tested against the installed ste-lint: API, idempotent, tuple, dict, parse, callable, iterable, dispatch, mutate, cache, schema, regex, glob, metadata and boolean all score zero. 'The API is here' and 'Runs are idempotent' are clean. What ste-lint flags is PASSIVE VOICE and a short list of ordinary verbs it has a preferred synonym for -- 'This module provides an API' fires on 'provides' while 'This module gives an API' is clean. STE did not cause the circumlocution the author rejected. THE SURVIVING CASE, MEASURED. (1) Its gate is MAX_STE_PER_100_WORDS = 2.5, a RATE, so cutting words while holding violations flat makes the score worse: the 14-module package scored 0.12 before a 60 per cent prose cut and 0.98 after, 8 times worse for strictly better prose. Both pass 2.5, so STE was never blocking the good prose -- it points the wrong way rather than failing. (2) Its active-voice mandate penalises the shortest docstring phrasing, where the actor is the module and naming it is padding. Per sentence over the real arm: STE flagged 6 sentences in the original and 4 of those 6 were sentences the R9-10 cut tests condemn independently -- two justification tails, one verbose ordering, one table described in prose. After the rewrite it flags 5, and all of them are the improved sentences, every one passive: 'Malformed reports are skipped', 'Entries missing a path, size or team are counted and skipped', 'Rows are keyed on team, total and quota, so runs are idempotent'. So STE is REDUNDANT WHERE IT IS RIGHT and WRONG WHERE IT DIFFERS: every true positive it found is already caught by R9-10, and its remaining disagreements are all cases where it prefers the longer sentence. That, not the jargon claim, is why it goes. TWO RULES SALVAGED into SKILL.md: one idea per sentence, and one word for one thing WITH the added clause that the word is the identifier the code uses -- the author's own rewrite said 'unassigned' where the code says 'unattributed' 26 times, which is the drift that clause exists to stop. Removal touches SKILL.md, README.md and verify.py, which drops gradeProse, the --ste-lint flag, MAX_STE_PER_100_WORDS and STE_LINT_DEFAULT; splitByKind becomes discoverPython and verify.py no longer reads prose at all.

choice: state cut tests plus a list of what earns a place
condition: derived from one reviewer on one package; the positive list is what survived, not what was predicted
note: Derived by red-teaming seven candidate prose rules against a working 14-module package and correcting them against the author's own rewrites. FOUR CUT TESTS: visible in the file; negation is a bug, an absurdity or an implementation nobody would ship; explains a language feature; goes stale unchecked. The negation test unifies three separate rules that were proposed apart -- 'asserts the absence of a bug', 'negation is absurd', and the author's 'it would be completely insane for a report scanner to break catastrophically like this'. It correctly SPARES sentences that look similar: 'Units are powers of 1024' survives because powers of 1000 is a real alternative, and 'Unparseable lines are counted and skipped' survives because fail-on-first-bad-line is a real design that the V3 arm shipped. FOUR COMPRESSIONS: name the property rather than explain it (idempotent); state an ordering as its sort key, because prose cannot say whether a multi-level sort is one composite key or two separate sorts, nor that the tie-break runs ascending while the numbers run descending; the summary names what the code produces by its real name; stop at the fact. SIX THINGS THAT EARN A BODY: an ordering or tie-break, a unit or nullability or provenance the annotation cannot carry, where the leftover and default and failure cases go, a sample of concrete text, a constraint from outside the program, and a guarantee a caller needs. The positive list is load-bearing: seven subtractive tests with no counterweight drive every docstring to a bare summary line. MEASURED: prose across the package fell from 676 to 272 words, 60 per cent, with total lines flat at 129 to 124 because the prose that left was replaced by samples. All six gate checks passed and the program ran unchanged. Three modules were untouched -- both entry points and the already-rewritten quotas.py -- so the tests bite on the middle of a package and leave its edges alone.

choice: NAR011 ships; NAR012 was built, measured and withdrawn
note: Two checks were written for the mechanical parts of R9-08 and R9-10. NAR011 flags a docstring whose body is indented past the docstring's own column, which ruff format then flattens, destroying a pasted sample. FIRST VERSION WAS WRONG: it compared the body against column 0, so every function docstring tripped it -- 88 findings across six packages, almost all false. Comparing against the docstring literal's col_offset fixed it: 0 findings across all six real packages and the skill's own four tools, and it agrees with ruff format on all three test forms, firing on an all-indented module docstring and on a function docstring indented past the def, and staying silent on an anchored block that ruff leaves alone. NAR012 was to flag a backticked identifier in a docstring that no name in the file matches, aimed at the unassigned-versus-unattributed drift. MEASURED AND WITHDRAWN: it fired on `Car` in an illustrative example, on `tomllib` named as a stdlib module, and on `backticked` used as an ordinary word. Prose legitimately names things that are not in the file, so absence is the wrong signal, and the drift it targets is semantic rather than mechanical. That clause stays review judgement under R9-09. A third trap needs no new check: a blank line inside a pasted real file becomes a whitespace-only line once the block is indented, which ruff already reports as W293.

choice: OPEN: R9-01's optional fields make a natural-column dedup key silently wrong in SQLite
condition: second-order consequence of a rule, not a defect in it
note: R9-01 says a parsed record states only what its input carried, so on V5 a billed_not_found finding carries team=None and a found_not_billed finding carries monthly_cents=None. Those records are then the key for the no-double-insert requirement. VERIFIED: a SQLite UNIQUE index spanning a nullable column does not deduplicate. Three identical INSERT OR IGNORE of a row whose team is NULL, under UNIQUE(kind, rid, cents, team), produce THREE rows; the same insert under UNIQUE(kind, rid) produces one. SQLite holds two NULLs distinct in a UNIQUE index. All three V5 arms avoided it by different routes -- base with a (kind, resource_id) primary key and ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, full with UNIQUE (kind, resource_id) and INSERT OR IGNORE, skill with a sha256 digest of every field as the key -- and only skill named it, calling it 'the one non-obvious correctness trap in the task'. Worth carrying into the skill because the next program that keys a store on a record with optional fields meets it, and the failure is silent: the gate passes, the program runs, and the table grows a row per run.

note: Raised by the author against v5 full's rules.py:73, canonicaliseRegion(region, reconcile_rules) returning reconcile_rules.region_aliases.get(region, region), with the objection that this should use get in place. THE AUTHOR RULED ON ALL SEVEN CASES INDIVIDUALLY before the rule was written. INLINE: canonicaliseRegion (a dict .get with a default), isBillingFile and isScanFile (path.name.lower().endswith(SUFFIX)), pathsIn (sorted over iterdir filtered by is_file). KEEP: normalizeName (_NAME_SEPARATORS.sub('-', name.strip().lower()), the PEP 503 fold), findReports (sorted over iterdir filtered by is_file AND is_report), _normalise (posixpath.normpath(path.strip()) if path.strip() else path). The author's stated principle: 'It is about the complexity of the line. Hiding a single .get call is not worth the misdirection, hiding _NAME_SEPARATORS.sub("-", name.strip().lower()) is fine.' findReports and pathsIn settle the boundary because one token separates them -- findReports composes isReport, a concept from the problem, and the name of the whole states that the two conditions belong together. MEASUREMENT THAT SHAPED THE SCOPE: one-line functions are not a guided-arm problem. Functions whose body is a single return or expression: base arms 34, 37 and 31 per cent, guided arms 12, 18 and 14 per cent, so the style already halves them. Narrowing to module-level functions forwarding to exactly one attribute of one parameter gives seven hits across eight packages and five of the seven are in unguided base arms. NO CHECKER SHIPS, for the reason NAR012 was withdrawn earlier the same day: six of the seven hits are legitimate, so a mechanical rule is six false positives in seven.
